## The model {#sec-model}

The instance, the plans and the Pareto front, as fixed in §1 of the note. The papers define the
model informally; the note makes plans precise (routes, journeys, capacity, waiting) and the Lean
development transcribes that definition. Definitions are the trusted interface of the whole
formalization: every theorem below is about these objects.

### Instances {#node-s1-1}

**Lean** [Lean definition]{.badge .ok} · **Note** [definition]{.badge .informal}

::: {.from-paper}
**From the original paper** (Quemy & Schoenauer, EvoCOP 2015, §2.1 *Instances*, HAL preprint hal-01109777v1, pp. 2–3).

> Let us introduce some notations related to the planning problem briefly presented in the
> introduction: a MultiZenoTravel instance (Figure 1) is defined by the following elements:
>
> – $n$ central cities, organized as a clique in which every node is connected to $C_I$ and $C_G$, respectively the initial city and the goal city.\
> – $c \in (\mathbb R^+)^n$, where $c_i$ is the cost for landing in $C_i$.\
> – $D \in (\mathbb R^+)^{n\times n}$, where $D_{ij}$ is the flying time between $C_i$ and $C_j$.\
> – $d^I \in (\mathbb R^+)^n$, where $d^I_i$ is the flying time between $C_I$ and $C_i$.\
> – $d^G \in (\mathbb R^+)^n$, where $d^G_i$ is the flying time between $C_i$ and $C_G$.\
> – $p$ planes, initially in $C_I$, that have a capacity of an unique person.\
> – $t$ persons, initially in $C_I$.
>
> As said, the goal is to carry all $t$ persons, initially in $c_I$, to $c_G$ using $p$ planes,
> minimizing both the makespan and the cost of the plan. In order to ease the identification of the
> true Pareto Front, a symmetry constraint is added: $\forall i \in [1, n], d^I_i = d^G_i$ and from
> thereon we will refer to a unique vector $d$.
:::

::: {.from-paper}
**From the original paper** (Quemy, Schoenauer & Dreo, arXiv:2304.14659v1, §2.1 *Instances*).

> Let us introduce some notations related to the planning problem briefly presented in the
> introduction: a non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel instance (Figure 1) is defined by the following
> elements: […] $d\in(\mathbb{R}^{+})^{n}$, where $d_{i}$ is the flying time between $C_{I}$ and
> $C_{i}$. $\bar{d}\in(\mathbb{R}^{+})^{n}$, where $\bar{d}_{i}$ is the flying time between $C_{i}$
> and $C_{G}$. […]
>
> An instance of the symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel problem is an instance such that $d=\bar{d}$.
> […]
>
> Figure 2 illustrates an admissible solution. Note that the makespan for a plan is not necessarily the
> largest sum of the flights' duration as some planes might have to wait for others.
:::

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.1).

* Cities: $C_I$ (initial) and $C_G$ (goal), the *hubs*, and central cities $1,\dots,n$.
* Flights are undirected: an existing flight joins two distinct cities and has one duration, used in both
  directions. $C_I$–$i$ lasts $d_i \ge 0$, $i$–$C_G$ lasts $\bar d_i \ge 0$, and a central flight $i$–$j$
  ($i \ne j$), if it exists, lasts $d_{ij} = d_{ji} \ge 0$. There is no flight $C_I$–$C_G$.
  $\mathrm{dur}(a,b)$ denotes the duration of the flight $a$–$b$.
* Landing in central city $i$ costs $c_i \ge 0$; landing in a hub is free.
* $p \ge 1$ planes and $t \ge p$ passengers start in $C_I$ at time 0. A plane carries at most one passenger.
* Durations and times lie in an archimedean ordered field $\mathbb K$ ($\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$), so that
  $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ is defined. From §7 on, durations are integers.

**In Lean.** `Network` holds the durations `d`, `dbar` and an arbitrary table `dc` of central flights; costs are a separate argument `c : Fin n → ℕ`. Durations, costs and times are natural numbers (format v1); `Cert.check_sound_rat` extends the checker's soundness to rational times.

**Lean** `ZenoFront.Network` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- The flight network: durations between `C_I` and each city (`d`), between `C_G` and each city
(`dbar`), and between central cities (`dc`, arbitrary). -/
structure Network (n : ℕ) where
  d : Fin n → ℕ
  dbar : Fin n → ℕ
  dc : Fin n → Fin n → ℕ
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean`, lines 87–92](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean#L87-L92){.lean-src}

:::

### Plans, cost and makespan {#node-s1-2}

**Lean** [Lean definition]{.badge .ok} · **Note** [definition]{.badge .informal}

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.2).

**Definition (plan).** A plan on a finite set $Q$ of planes (all $p$ planes unless stated otherwise)
consists of

1. for every plane $k \in Q$, a *route*: a finite sequence of *legs* $(k,1),\dots,(k,\nu_k)$, where leg
   $(k,j)$ uses an existing flight joining $v_{k,j-1}$ and $v_{k,j}$, flown from $v_{k,j-1}$ to $v_{k,j}$,
   and departs at time $e_{k,j}$, with $v_{k,0} = C_I$, $e_{k,1} \ge 0$ and
   $e_{k,j+1} \ge a_{k,j} := e_{k,j} + \mathrm{dur}(v_{k,j-1}, v_{k,j})$;
2. for every passenger $\pi$, a *journey*: a non-empty sequence of legs whose first leg departs from $C_I$,
   whose last leg arrives in $C_G$, and in which each leg departs from the city where the previous one
   arrives, no earlier than that arrival, and, if both are legs of the same plane, at a later position of
   its route;
3. *capacity*: the journeys are pairwise disjoint, and none repeats a leg.

Below, "flight" also means a leg when no confusion is possible. The plan is *feasible* if every route ends in
$C_G$ ($\nu_k \ge 1$ and $v_{k,\nu_k} = C_G$). Its *cost*
$C = \sum_{k,j} c(v_{k,j})$ sums the landing costs of all flights (hubs are free). Its *makespan*
$M = \max_k a_{k,\nu_k}$ is the time at which the last plane reaches $C_G$ for the last time. $\mathcal A$
is the set of pairs $(C, M)$ of feasible plans.

Waiting is implicit: a departure may be later than the preceding arrival, for planes and for passengers.
Boarding and debarking are instantaneous: a passenger changing planes debarks when its flight arrives and
boards when the next one departs, and the only constraint is the time inequality of item 2. Several planes
may be in a city at once.

*Sequence order.* "First" and "last" refer to positions in a journey or in a route. With zero durations
several events can share a time; the sequences fix their order, and every argument below reads them this
way.

A plan is *event-ordered* if its legs have a total order $\prec$ that extends every route and every journey
and along which departure times do not decrease. Lemma 6.8 and Corollary 6.10 use this notion, and
Statement 1.2 relates it to PDDL; Theorem 6.9 does not need it. If every flight has a positive
duration, every plan is event-ordered: in a route or a journey the next leg departs after the previous one
arrives, hence strictly after it departs, so sorting legs by departure time extends both. Plans of the PDDL
domain are event-ordered too (Statement 1.2). With zero durations a plan can fail to be: a passenger may ride
a later leg of one plane and then an earlier leg of another at the same instant, in a cycle of dependencies
that no execution in time realises. Such plans do not change the front (Corollary 6.10).

The *flight time* of plane $k$ is $F_k = \sum_j \mathrm{dur}(f_{k,j})$. Its flights are sequential, so
$F_k \le a_{k,\nu_k} \le M$.

*Planes ending anywhere.* In the variant of Theorem 4.9, every plan counts (routes need not end in $C_G$ and
may be empty), journeys still end in $C_G$, and the makespan $M'$ is the largest arrival time over all legs;
there is at least one leg since $t \ge 1$. $\mathcal A'$ is the set of pairs $(C, M')$ of all plans.

**In Lean.** A plan gives every plane a list of legs (`Leg`: from, to, departure, arrival, passenger). `Feasible` requires routes chained from `C_I` at time ≥ 0 and ending in `C_G`, legs of exact duration, and every passenger's legs ordered into a route from `C_I` to `C_G`; capacity one holds by construction, since a leg names at most one passenger.

**Lean** `ZenoFront.Plan` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- A plan: the legs of every plane, in flight order. -/
abbrev Plan (n t p : ℕ) := Fin p → List (Leg n t)
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean`, lines 84–85](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean#L84-L85){.lean-src}

**Lean** `ZenoFront.Feasible` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- A feasible plan: every plane is feasible, and the legs carrying each passenger form, in some
order, a route from `C_I` at time `0` that ends in `C_G`. -/
structure Feasible (N : Network n) (P : Plan n t p) : Prop where
  planes : ∀ k, PlaneFeasible N (P k)
  pax : ∀ π, ∃ route : List (Leg n t), route.Perm (paxLegs P π) ∧ IsRoute .ci 0 route ∧
    finalLoc .ci route = .cg
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean`, lines 155–160](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/Plan.lean#L155-L160){.lean-src}

**Lean** `ZenoFront.achievable` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- The (cost, makespan) pairs of the feasible plans. -/
def achievable (N : Network n) (c : Fin n → ℕ) (t p : ℕ) : Set (ℕ × ℕ) :=
  {x | ∃ P : Plan n t p, Feasible N P ∧ (planCost c P, planMakespan P) = x}
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Checker.lean`, lines 48–50](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/Checker.lean#L48-L50){.lean-src}

:::

::: {.strengthen}
**What the note makes precise.** Neither paper defines a plan. Both reason with flight *patterns*
(P1–P3; $A$, $\bar A$, $B$, $\bar B$) and treat waiting informally. The note's definition, and its Lean
transcription, allow every behaviour a planner could produce: central flights of any duration,
waiting anywhere, hand-offs anywhere, zero durations. Every lower bound below is proved against
*all* such plans, not against pattern plans.
:::

### Statement 1.2 (PDDL correspondence) {#node-statement-1-2}

**Lean** [informal]{.badge .informal} · **Note** [sketch]{.badge .informal}

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.3).

**Statement 1.2 (PDDL correspondence, S).** A plan of the domain under ε-separation yields a plan of §1.2
with the same cost and a makespan at most its `total-time`: each plane's `fly` actions in time order form
its route, each person's flights between `board` and `debark` form its journey, and `libre` gives capacity
one; ordering the `fly` actions by start time (ties by the plan's order of actions) shows that this plan is
event-ordered. Conversely, an event-ordered plan of §1.2 with makespan $M$ yields PDDL plans with
`total-time` at most $M + K\varepsilon$, where $K$ is its number of `fly`, `board` and `debark` actions:
list the actions in the event order (each `board` just before its leg, each `debark` just after) and delay
the $r$-th one by $r\varepsilon$. So the PDDL front tends to the front of event-ordered plans, which is
$\mathcal F$ under (S) and (A1), and under (S) and (AΔ) (the plans of Theorem 4.1 are event-ordered, Lemma
6.8(c); Corollaries 4.8 and 4.12), and under (A1-NS)
(Corollary 6.10). The model's makespan is thus the PDDL makespan in the limit ε → 0, which is
what ZenoSolver reports. Whether PDDL planners and VAL accept zero-duration actions is not checked here. This
is argued, not formalised.

:::

### Assumptions {#node-s1-4}

**Lean** [Lean definition]{.badge .ok} · **Note** [definition]{.badge .informal}

::: {.from-paper}
**From the original paper** (Quemy & Schoenauer, EvoCOP 2015, §2.2 *Pareto Optimal Plans*, HAL preprint hal-01109777v1, pp. 3–4).

> Let us make another simplifying assumption:\
> **Assumption A1**: $\forall (i, j) \in [1, n]^2, d_i + d_j < d_{ij}$. Then the following holds.
>
> **Proposition**: Pareto-optimal plans are plans where exactly $2t - p$ (possibly identical) central
> cities are used by a flight.
>
> **Proof**: Consider a plan where a person flies from $C_i$ to $C_j$. Using the same plane, the same
> person could fly instead from $C_i$ to $C_G$, and the plane would return empty to $C_j$. The plan
> could continue unchanged from thereon: because of the hypothesis on makespans, the needed resource
> would be in $C_j$ on time. Moreover, the total cost is unchanged, and the total makespan is lower or
> equal to the original one: the new plan thus Pareto-dominates the original one.
>
> Iterating the same reasoning for each person, and each empty plane, we conclude that there are no
> flights between central cities in Pareto-optimal plans. Thus bringing the $t$ persons from $C_I$ to
> $C_G$ will amount to carry each person through one central city: $t$ flights will be needed from
> $C_I$ to one $C_i$, then $t$ flights from $C_i$ to $C_G$. Finally, because planes do not need to come
> back from $C_G$ in the end, only $t - p$ flights back empty will be needed, possibly through some
> different central cities – hence the result. $\square$
>
> *Footnote 3 (on Assumption A1):* This might look unrealistic in real-world logistic domain. However,
> we hypothesize that the proposition still holds with the weaker condition that for any cities
> $C_i, C_j, C_k$ (if we state the cost of $C_I$ and $C_G$ are respectively $C_0$ and $C_{n+1}$),
> $d_{ik} \le d_{ij} + d_{jk}$ (triangle inequality).
:::

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.4).

Used only where stated.

* (S) symmetry: $d_i = \bar d_i$ for all $i$.
* (A1) central flights are useless: under (S), $d_{ij} \ge d_i + d_j$ for every existing central flight.
  This is the EvoCOP 2015 assumption (stated there with $>$).
* (A1-NS) $d_{ij} \ge \min(d_i + d_j,\ \bar d_i + \bar d_j)$ for every existing central flight.
* (AΔ) triangle inequality for the flights that exist: $\mathrm{dur}(a,b) \le \mathrm{dur}(a,x) + \mathrm{dur}(x,b)$
  whenever the three flights exist.
* (AΔ-path) for all central $i$ and $z$: $\bar d_i \le d_i + d_z + \bar d_z$ and
  $d_i \le \bar d_i + \bar d_z + d_z$. A hub leg of $i$ is no longer than the detour through $z$ and the
  other hub. (S) implies it, and (AΔ) implies it when the central flight $i$–$z$ exists.

**In Lean.** (S) is the hypothesis `N.dbar = N.d`. `Network.A1` is `d_i + d_j ≤ dc i j` (the paper's strict `<` weakened to `≤`), `Network.A1NS` is `min(d_i + d_j, d̄_i + d̄_j) ≤ dc i j`.

**Lean** `ZenoFront.Network.A1` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- Assumption (A1): central flights are useless, `dc i j ≥ d i + d j` (under (S)). -/
def Network.A1 (N : Network n) : Prop := ∀ i j, N.d i + N.d j ≤ N.dc i j
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Converse.lean`, lines 51–52](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/Converse.lean#L51-L52){.lean-src}

**Lean** `ZenoFront.Network.A1NS` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- Assumption (A1-NS): a central flight is no shorter than a detour through one of the hubs. -/
def Network.A1NS (N : Network n) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j, min (N.d i + N.d j) (N.dbar i + N.dbar j) ≤ N.dc i j
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/NonSymmetric.lean`, lines 44–46](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/NonSymmetric.lean#L44-L46){.lean-src}

:::

### Fronts {#node-s1-5}

**Lean** [Lean definition]{.badge .ok} · **Note** [definition]{.badge .informal}

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.5).

For points $y, z \in \mathbb K^2$ (cost, makespan), $y \preceq z$, *$y$ weakly dominates $z$*, if
$y \le z$ componentwise. For $\mathcal S \subseteq \mathbb K^2$, $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$ is the set of
$z \in \mathcal S$ such that no $y \in \mathcal S$ other than $z$ has $y \preceq z$. The *front* is
$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A$.

**In Lean.** `IsParetoFront S F`: the listed points are in `S`, every point of `S` is weakly dominated by a listed point, and the list is an antichain. `IsParetoFront.mem_iff_minimal` shows that it lists exactly the minimal elements of `S`.

**Lean** `ZenoFront.IsParetoFront` [Lean definition]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- `F` is the Pareto front of `S` (for the product order on (cost, makespan)): its points are in
`S`, weakly dominate every point of `S`, and are pairwise incomparable. -/
structure IsParetoFront {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α] (S : Set α) (F : List α) : Prop where
  achieved : ∀ x ∈ F, x ∈ S
  dominates : ∀ y ∈ S, ∃ x ∈ F, x ≤ y
  antichain : F.Pairwise fun a b => ¬ a ≤ b ∧ ¬ b ≤ a
```

[`lean/ZenoFront/Checker.lean`, lines 52–57](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/d90b3006488a75365faf437a9bae79a551384196/lean/ZenoFront/Checker.lean#L52-L57){.lean-src}

:::

### Notation {#node-notation}

**Lean** [informal]{.badge .informal} · **Note** [definition]{.badge .informal}

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.5).

**Notation.** $s = 2t - p$, so $s \ge p$ and $s \equiv p \pmod 2$; $\kappa = \lceil s/p\rceil$;
$d_{\max} = \max_i d_i$. For multisets of central cities: $Y(i)$ is the multiplicity of $i$, $|Y|$ the size,
$\mathrm{supp}\,Y$ the support, $Y + Z$ the sum, $Z \le Y$ inclusion and $Y - Z$ the difference for
$Z \le Y$; $c(Y) = \sum_{w\in Y} c_w$, $\delta(Y) = \sum_{w\in Y} d_w$, $\bar\delta(Y) = \sum_{w\in Y} \bar d_w$,
and under (S) the *load* $\ell(Y) = 2\delta(Y)$. A *partition* of $X$ over a finite set $Q$ of planes is a
family $(X_k)_{k \in Q}$ (one group per plane, possibly empty) with $\sum_{k\in Q} X_k = X$. Unless stated
otherwise $Q$ is the set of all $p$ planes, written $X_1,\dots,X_p$; definitions and results of §2 hold for
any $Q$, with $p$ replaced by $|Q|$.

:::

### Lemma 1.1 (dominating subset) {#node-lemma-1-1}

**Lean** [informal]{.badge .informal} (parts in Lean) · **Note** [proof in the note]{.badge .informal}

::: {.our-work}
**Statement** (theory note, §1.5).

**Lemma 1.1 (dominating subset).** Let $\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S \subseteq \mathbb K^2$ with
$\mathcal S'$ finite and every point of $\mathcal S$ weakly dominated by a point of $\mathcal S'$. Then
$\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'$, and every point of $\mathcal S$ is weakly dominated
by a point of $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple" title="Proof (theory note)"}
*Proof.* Let $z \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$. Some $y \in \mathcal S'$ has $y \preceq z$, so $y = z$, and
$z$ is minimal in $\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S$. Let $z \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'$ and $y \in \mathcal S$
with $y \preceq z$. Some $y' \in \mathcal S'$ has $y' \preceq y \preceq z$, so $y' = z$ and then $y = z$.
Finally, for $z \in \mathcal S$, take $y \in \mathcal S'$ with $y \preceq z$ and a $\preceq$-minimal element
of the finite set $\{y' \in \mathcal S' : y' \preceq y\}$; it lies in $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S' = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$. $\square$
:::
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
*Proof.* Let $z \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$. Some $y \in \mathcal S'$ has $y \preceq z$, so $y = z$, and
$z$ is minimal in $\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S$. Let $z \in \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'$ and $y \in \mathcal S$
with $y \preceq z$. Some $y' \in \mathcal S'$ has $y' \preceq y \preceq z$, so $y' = z$ and then $y = z$.
Finally, for $z \in \mathcal S$, take $y \in \mathcal S'$ with $y \preceq z$ and a $\preceq$-minimal element
of the finite set $\{y' \in \mathcal S' : y' \preceq y\}$; it lies in $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S' = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$. $\square$
:::

**In Lean.** The first claim, `Min S = Min S'`, is machine-checked without the finiteness hypothesis. The last claim (every point is dominated by a minimal one) uses finiteness and is not stated in Lean.

**Formalised parts.** These declarations cover part of the statement; the node keeps the status of the note.

*Part* `ZenoFront.minimal_iff_of_subset_of_dominated` [machine-checked]{.badge .ok}

```lean
/-- If `A ⊆ A′` and every point of `A′` is weakly dominated by a point of `A`, the two sets have
the same minimal elements. -/
theorem minimal_iff_of_subset_of_dominated {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α] {A A' : Set α}
    (hsub : A ⊆ A') (hdom : ∀ y ∈ A', ∃ x ∈ A, x ≤ y) (x : α) :
    Minimal (· ∈ A) x ↔ Minimal (· ∈ A') x := …
```
